passages.t: The temple sermon: a den of robbers
passages.happening:
God sends Jeremiah to stand in the gate of the LORD's house and speak to everyone who comes in to worship (verse 2). ‘Correct your ways and deeds, and I will let you live in this place’ (verse 3). ‘Do not trust in deceptive words’ (verse 4). The people chant three times that this is the temple of the LORD, as if the words could keep them safe (verse 4).

If they really change, act justly, stop oppressing the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow, stop shedding innocent blood and following other gods, then God will let them live in the land (verses 5 to 7). But will they steal, murder, commit adultery and perjury, burn incense to Baal, and then come and stand in God's house and claim they are safe (verses 9 and 10)? ‘Has this house, which bears My Name, become a den of robbers in your sight?’ (verse 11).

They are to go to Shiloh, where God first set his name, and see what he did to it (verse 12). ‘Therefore what I did to Shiloh I will now do to the house that bears My Name’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 26 dates this sermon to the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign, about 609 or 608 BC. Josiah, the reforming king, had just been killed at Megiddo, and his reforms were quickly coming undone. Chapter 26 tells what happened next: priests, prophets and people seized Jeremiah and demanded his death.

The temple gate was where crowds entered for festivals and sacrifices, the most public pulpit in Judah. Worshipers often recited words at the gate; some psalms ask who may enter God's house and answer with the demands of justice. Jeremiah's hearers chanted a phrase of confidence instead, as if the words themselves guaranteed safety.

A den of robbers is the cave where thieves hide between raids. The people did their wrongs outside and ran to the temple to feel safe. Shiloh, in Ephraim, was where the tabernacle stood in the days of Eli and Samuel. It had long been a ruin. The first hearers knew God had let his own house fall before.
passages.later: When Jesus cleared the temple, he joined Isaiah's words to the den of robbers of verse 11 (Matthew 21:13). A psalm remembers Shiloh: ‘He abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh’ (Psalm 78:60).
passages.asks: The people treated the temple as a hiding place for their wrongs. Ask whether you have used church, prayer or a religious habit as a place to feel safe without changing. And ask how you treat the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow near you.

passages.t: Do not pray for them, and obedience before sacrifice
passages.happening:
God tells Jeremiah not to pray for these people, for he will not listen (verse 16). Does Jeremiah not see what they are doing? ‘The sons gather wood, the fathers light the fire, and the women knead the dough to make cakes for the Queen of Heaven’ (verse 18). But is it God they are hurting? ‘Is it not themselves they spite, to their own shame?’ (verse 19).

God says they may add their burnt offerings to their other sacrifices and eat the meat themselves (verse 21). When he brought their fathers out of Egypt, he did not merely command offerings (verse 22). ‘But this is what I commanded them: Obey Me, and I will be your God, and you will be My people’ (verse 23). Yet they did not listen. ‘They went backward and not forward’ (verse 24).

God sent his prophets again and again, and they would not listen (verses 25 and 26). Jeremiah is to say, ‘Truth has perished; it has disappeared from their lips’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The Queen of Heaven was a goddess, most likely the Mesopotamian Ishtar or a related goddess such as Astarte, linked with the evening star, fertility and war. Her worship was a family affair. Children gathered wood, fathers lit fires and women baked cakes. The whole household was drawn in.

To eat the meat of burnt offerings was a bitter joke. Burnt offerings were wholly burned to God. God says they may as well eat them, since none of it pleases him.

The prophets before Jeremiah had already said that God wanted obedience more than sacrifice. Samuel told Saul so. Jeremiah stands in that line.
passages.later: Samuel told Saul, ‘Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice’ (1 Samuel 15:22). Hosea says the same: ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice’ (Hosea 6:6).
passages.hard:
In verses 22 and 23, does God say he never commanded sacrifices, even though Leviticus is full of them?

The Hebrew of verse 22 can be read as a flat statement that God did not speak to the fathers about burnt offerings when he brought them out of Egypt. Taken alone, that seems to contradict the sacrificial laws. Many interpreters see a Hebrew way of giving emphasis, not merely this but that, which is how the BSB renders it: God did not merely command sacrifices. Others note that the first word God gave at Sinai was the call to obey and the covenant promise, with the sacrificial laws following. Either way, the verse does not reject worship. It rejects worship cut off from obedience.
passages.asks: God says the people went backward and not forward. Ask in what part of your life you have been going backward. And ask whether your worship and your daily obedience belong to the same life.

passages.happening:
Jerusalem is told to cut off her hair and throw it away and raise a lament on the bare heights, for the LORD has rejected the generation of his wrath (verse 29). The people have set up their abominations in God's own house (verse 30).

‘They have built the high places of Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom so they could burn their sons and daughters in the fire’ (verse 31). It was something God never commanded, ‘nor did it even enter My mind’ (verse 31).

So the place will be called the Valley of Slaughter, and the dead will be buried there until there is no room (verse 32). God will silence in Judah's cities ‘the sounds of joy and gladness and the voices of the bride and bridegroom’ (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Topheth was a site in the Valley of Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem. Children were killed there as offerings, a practice the law forbade. The chapter names it and does not describe it, and these notes do the same.

God's words in verse 31 are among the strongest in the Bible. Child sacrifice was not something he had commanded or even thought of. Whatever the people believed about it, God disowns it completely.

The Valley of Hinnom, in Hebrew Ge-hinnom, later gave its name to Gehenna, the place of final judgment in Jesus' teaching.

The silence of the bride and bridegroom is the end of ordinary joy. No weddings, no feasts, no future families.
passages.later: The law had forbidden it: ‘You must not give any of your children to be sacrificed to Molech’ (Leviticus 18:21). Josiah had defiled Topheth so that no one could use it (2 Kings 23:10).
passages.hard:
Children were burned at Topheth. How should a reader carry that?

The chapter names the horror and gives God's verdict: it never entered his mind. It is condemned as evil, never offered as a lesson about the children. No child's suffering is a verdict on the child, and nothing in this chapter says otherwise.

Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God says child sacrifice never entered his mind. Ask what it means that God is so wholly against harm done to children. And ask what you could do to protect children in your church or town.
